name: The Third Man argument against Plato's theory of Ideas
plain_explanation: If a particular man is a man because he resembles the ideal Man, then that resemblance itself needs explaining -- which requires a still more ideal 'third man' that both the particular man and the ideal Man resemble, and so on without end.
precise_definition: Aristotle's argument, already foreshadowed in Plato's own Parmenides, that when several individuals share a predicate, this sharing cannot be explained by their all resembling a further individual of the same kind (however 'ideal'), since that would require a yet more ideal exemplar to explain the new resemblance, generating an infinite regress.
why_it_mattered: It shows decisively, in Russell's judgement, that shared predicates cannot be explained by resemblance to a super-particular 'Idea' of the same logical type as ordinary things.
historical_origin: Already present in Plato's own self-criticism in the Parmenides; developed as a formal argument by Aristotle against the theory of Ideas.
examples: Socrates is both a man and an animal, raising the question whether the Ideal Man is also an Ideal Animal, and if so, whether there must be as many ideal animals as species
competing_positions: Plato's theory of Ideas, which the argument is directed against
influence_on_later_thinkers: Left the problem of universals unresolved rather than solved, since Aristotle's own alternative doctrine was, in Russell's view, far from clear -- 'it was this lack of clarity that made possible the medieval controversy between nominalists and realists.'
